metadata.title: How Blind Journal protects your writing
metadata.description: See how Blind Journal encrypts journal entries in your browser, separates sign-in from journal unlocking, and stores only protected journal data on the server.

hero.title: How Blind Journal protects your writing
hero.body: Blind Journal is designed so your journal can be stored remotely without giving the server what it needs to read it. Your browser derives the keys, encrypts entries before they are sent, and decrypts them when you open them again. The server manages accounts, sessions, and storage, but journal content reaches it already encrypted and the key material needed to read it stays in your browser.

bigPicture.title: Where does my journal get encrypted?
bigPicture.body: While you are reading or editing an entry, the readable version exists in your browser. Before the title or body leaves the browser, Blind Journal encrypts it. The server receives the encrypted version instead of the readable entry.
bigPicture.httpsBody: HTTPS protects information while it travels between your browser and the server. Blind Journal encrypts the journal before that trip begins, so HTTPS carries an already-encrypted entry to the server.

authentication.title: How can the server sign me in without being able to read my journal?
authentication.body: Your passphrase supports two different jobs: proving to the server that you are allowed to sign in, and unlocking your journal. Blind Journal keeps those jobs separate. When you enter your passphrase, your browser derives separate key material for authentication and for unlocking the journal.
authentication.separationBody: The authentication key is sent to the server so it can verify your sign-in and create a session. The journal-unlock key stays in your browser. It does not directly encrypt every entry: each entry gets its own key, and the journal-unlock key is used to protect and unlock those entry keys. Because the two purposes are separate, the information the server uses to sign you in does not give it the ability to decrypt your journal. Your passphrase itself is never sent to the server.

saving.title: What happens when I press Save?
saving.body: Every journal entry gets its own random encryption key. When you press Save, your browser uses that key to encrypt the title and body, then protects the entry key itself using your journal-unlock key.
saving.storageBody: The server receives the encrypted entry, the protected entry key, and the basic record information needed to store and retrieve it. It never receives the readable entry or an unlocked entry key.
saving.openingTitle: What happens when I open it again?
saving.openingBody: The process runs in reverse. The server sends the encrypted entry and its protected key back to your browser. Your browser uses the journal-unlock key to unlock the entry key, then uses that entry key to decrypt the journal locally.

visibility.title: What can the server actually see?
visibility.body: Encryption protects your journal’s contents, not every part of using an online service. The server still needs information to manage accounts, authenticate requests, and store encrypted records. The important boundary is whether that information can be used to read the journal.

observable.identity: Account information: your username, display name, and internal account identifier.
observable.authentication: Sign-in information: the derived authentication key during account creation and sign-in, a one-way verifier, session records, and the public settings your browser needs to derive the same keys again later.
observable.records: Encrypted-entry information: entry identifiers, creation and update times, encrypted sizes, and record counts.
observable.operations: Normal network activity: requests, timing, access patterns, and IP-derived operational data.

private.journalKey: The key material used to unlock your journal.

visibility.summary: The server can know that encrypted journal data exists without having what it needs to turn that data back into your journal.

architecture.title: How does the whole system fit together?
architecture.body: Put together, each part has one job. The browser derives and keeps the keys needed to read your journal and handles encryption and decryption. The server handles accounts, authentication, sessions, authorization, and storage. The database stores the account information the service needs along with protected journal records.
architecture.flowBody: Saving moves protected data from the browser to the server and database. Opening an entry brings that protected data back to the browser, where it is unlocked and decrypted. The server stores the journal, but the browser holds what is needed to read it.

zeroKnowledge.title: Why is Blind Journal called zero knowledge?
zeroKnowledge.body: You may see Blind Journal described as a zero-knowledge application. Here, that means the server can authenticate you and store your journal without possessing the keys required to read it.
zeroKnowledge.limitsBody: It does not mean the server sees nothing. As described above, account information, encrypted-record metadata, and normal network activity remain visible. The key point is that the server can store and manage the journal without being able to decrypt its contents.

technicalDepth.title: Want to go deeper?
technicalDepth.body: This page explains the system at a conceptual level. The project README documents the cryptographic algorithms, key derivation, authentication protocol, encrypted record format, and security assumptions behind it.
